title: Install upstream ansible-core with pipx on RHEL 9
objective: Register RHEL, install a supported Python and pipx, create an isolated upstream ansible-core application, record and recreate its exact package baseline, restore its pin, and verify its provenance, content boundary, and runtime behavior.
coverAlt: pipx managing an isolated upstream ansible-core application environment and exposing commands on the current user's PATH
outcomes: Register RHEL and confirm its Red Hat service connections
Select a maintained upstream ansible-core and compatible control-node Python
Install Python 3.12 without replacing RHEL's platform Python
Install pipx in the current user's Python package directory
Persist the user application directory on PATH
Install upstream ansible-core from PyPI in a pipx-managed environment
Record and recreate the exact pipx application package baseline, then restore its pin
Verify isolation, content boundaries, and functional execution
validationBoundary: This proves that pipx owns an isolated upstream ansible-core application environment and that its exposed commands work on the local control node. It does not validate remote inventory, SSH connectivity, credentials, privilege escalation, network policy, or managed-host Python readiness.
nextActions: Save the pipx inventory, exact requirements, rebuild result, and pin status with the project or workstation notes that depend on it.
Use pipx as the sole owner for inspecting, upgrading, pinning, or removing this application environment.
Repeat the isolation, dependency, documentation, and ansible.builtin.ping checks after approved updates.
Validate inventory, transport, credentials, privilege escalation, and Python against a managed Linux host.

steps.label: System Baseline
steps.title: Inspect the clean RHEL environment
steps.alt: Terminal showing the RHEL 9 release, processor architecture, ansible-core RPM state, and default Python version
steps.explanation: Establish the operating-system, processor architecture, Ansible RPM state, and default Python version before selecting packages. This baseline distinguishes the later upstream installation from software already managed by RHEL.

commands.explanation: Reads the RHEL release file to identify the installed operating-system name and major release.
Reports the processor architecture, which determines which architecture-specific repositories and packages apply to the host.
Queries the RPM database for the RHEL-provided ansible-core package. A not-installed result confirms the clean package state expected here.
Shows the version behind RHEL's default python3 command before an additional interpreter is installed.

steps.expected: The host reports RHEL 9 and its architecture, confirms that the ansible-core RPM is absent, and displays the default Python version.
steps.note: This recording uses an aarch64 VM. Package architecture differs on x86_64 systems.
steps.troubleshooting: If the system is not RHEL 9, stop and use the guidance for that platform. If ansible-core is already installed through RPM, pip, pipx, or another environment, do not continue on this system; reset it or use a separate clean RHEL 9 environment so package ownership and PATH results remain unambiguous.

steps.label: Register RHEL
steps.title: Register RHEL with Red Hat services
steps.alt: RHEL terminal confirming successful connections to Red Hat services
steps.explanation: A registered RHEL system can retrieve protected content from Red Hat repositories. This demonstration uses an interactive Red Hat account login and keeps all credential input outside the published replay.

commands.explanation: Runs the Red Hat connector with administrative privileges. It registers the system with Subscription Management and connects it to Red Hat Lightspeed.

steps.expected: rhc reports successful connections to Red Hat Subscription Management and Red Hat Lightspeed and activates remote host configuration. The recorded client uses the former Red Hat Insights name in its output.
steps.note: Credential input is excluded from the replay. The neutral placeholders show where learners interact without exposing an account name or password.
steps.troubleshooting: Use the message returned by rhc connect to distinguish an interactive-login problem from a registration or service-connection failure.

recovery.symptom: No credential prompt appears
recovery.detail: Run rhc connect from an interactive terminal. A background process or non-interactive shell cannot accept the Red Hat account prompts.

recovery.symptom: Authentication or registration fails
recovery.detail: Confirm network access, DNS, proxy configuration, system time, and an active RHEL entitlement, then retry this registration step.
recovery.command: sudo rhc connect

steps.label: Verify Connection
steps.title: Verify the Red Hat connection
steps.alt: RHEL terminal showing active Subscription Management and Red Hat hosted inventory connections
steps.explanation: Registration should be confirmed independently before relying on protected repositories. The connection status separates a successful login from a usable registered system.

commands.explanation: Reports the system's current connections to Subscription Management, Red Hat Lightspeed, and remote host configuration services.

steps.expected: The recorded system is connected to Red Hat Subscription Management and Red Hat Lightspeed. The recorded client uses the former Red Hat Insights name, and remote host configuration may be inactive.
steps.note: Subscription Management is required for DNF repository access. Red Hat Lightspeed and remote host configuration are separate services; their state does not determine whether DNF can use subscribed repositories.
steps.troubleshooting: Read each rhc status line separately. Return to registration when Subscription Management is disconnected; do not treat an inactive Lightspeed or remote host configuration connection as a DNF repository failure.

recovery.symptom: Subscription Management is disconnected
recovery.detail: Return to the interactive registration step, confirm the entitled RHEL account and network path, then repeat the connection check.
recovery.command:
sudo rhc connect
sudo rhc status

recovery.symptom: Only Lightspeed or remote host configuration is inactive
recovery.detail: Continue with the DNF workflow when Subscription Management is connected. Investigate the other service only when the organization uses that capability.

steps.label: Check Repositories
steps.title: Review the enabled RHEL repositories
steps.alt: DNF output listing enabled RHEL BaseOS and AppStream repositories
steps.explanation: RHEL separates its operating-system foundation and application content into repositories. Both BaseOS and AppStream must be available before the package workflow begins.

commands.explanation: Lists repositories enabled in the system's Red Hat subscription configuration, including their full identifiers and status.
Shows the enabled repositories that DNF can currently use. The concise output makes BaseOS and AppStream easy to confirm.

steps.expected: Both the RHEL 9 BaseOS and AppStream RPM repositories appear as enabled.
steps.note: Repository IDs include the architecture. This recording uses aarch64; x86_64 systems show corresponding x86_64 repository IDs.
steps.troubleshooting: Compare both command outputs and identify exactly which architecture-specific BaseOS or AppStream repository is absent before changing repository configuration.

recovery.symptom: BaseOS or AppStream is not enabled
recovery.detail: Refresh the subscription data, enable the repository IDs matching this system's architecture, and repeat both repository-list commands from this step.
recovery.command:
sudo subscription-manager refresh
sudo subscription-manager repos \
  --enable="rhel-9-for-$(arch)-baseos-rpms" \
  --enable="rhel-9-for-$(arch)-appstream-rpms"

steps.label: Check Prerequisites
steps.title: Check the Python 3.12 and pipx prerequisites
steps.alt: Terminal checking Python 3.12 and pipx availability and listing the available Python packages
steps.explanation: Check whether Python 3.12 and pipx are already available, then confirm that the required Python packages can be obtained from RHEL. These checks establish exactly what the following installation steps need to add.

commands.command: command -v python3.12 || echo "Python 3.12 is not installed"
commands.explanation: Looks for a Python 3.12 executable and prints a clear baseline message when it is absent.

commands.command: command -v pipx || echo "pipx is not installed"
commands.explanation: Looks for the pipx executable and reports when it is not yet available on PATH.
Confirms that Python 3.12 and its matching pip package are available from the enabled RHEL repositories.

steps.expected: Python 3.12 and pipx are not found on the clean system, and DNF lists python3.12 and python3.12-pip as available packages.
steps.note: Consult the upstream compatibility matrix before choosing a Python and ansible-core pair. This demonstration uses ansible-core 2.21 with Python 3.12.
steps.troubleshooting: Treat a pre-existing Python or pipx command as an ownership check; treat a missing DNF package listing as a repository-metadata problem for this prerequisite step.

recovery.symptom: Python 3.12 or pipx is already available
recovery.detail: Record every matching executable and its owner before deciding whether the existing tools are suitable for this installation.
recovery.command:
type -a python3.12 pipx
command -v python3.12
command -v pipx

recovery.symptom: DNF cannot list the Python packages
recovery.detail: Confirm BaseOS and AppStream are enabled, refresh metadata, and repeat only this step's package-availability query.
recovery.command:
sudo dnf repolist --enabled
sudo dnf clean metadata
sudo dnf makecache
sudo dnf list --available python3.12 python3.12-pip

steps.label: Install Python
steps.title: Install and verify Python 3.12
steps.alt: DNF installing Python 3.12 followed by version checks for Python and pip
steps.explanation: Install the previously verified packages alongside RHEL's platform Python, then confirm that the new interpreter and its matching pip command start successfully. This supplies the compatible control-node runtime needed by ansible-core 2.21.

commands.explanation: Installs Python 3.12 and its matching pip package through DNF. Review and approve the transaction when prompted.
Confirms that the newly installed Python 3.12 interpreter starts successfully.
Confirms that pip is attached to Python 3.12 rather than RHEL's platform Python.

steps.expected: DNF completes the installation, Python reports version 3.12, and pip reports a location under the system's Python 3.12 package directory.
steps.note: Repository IDs and package architecture vary between aarch64 and x86_64 systems. Match the package names and behavior rather than the recorded architecture or exact patch version.
steps.troubleshooting: Use the failing command to distinguish a DNF installation problem from a Python or pip verification problem after the transaction.

recovery.symptom: The DNF transaction fails
recovery.detail: Refresh metadata and retry these Python packages without disabling signature verification, replacing the platform Python, or force-removing platform packages.
recovery.command:
sudo dnf clean metadata
sudo dnf makecache
sudo dnf install python3.12 python3.12-pip

recovery.symptom: The version checks fail after DNF completes
recovery.detail: Confirm both RPMs are installed, then repeat the Python and pip version commands from this step.
recovery.command:
rpm -q python3.12 python3.12-pip
python3.12 --version
python3.12 -m pip --version

steps.label: Install pipx
steps.title: Install pipx for the current user
steps.alt: Terminal installing pipx into the current user's Python package directory
steps.explanation: pipx is itself a Python command-line application. Python 3.12's pip retrieves it from the configured Python package index—PyPI in this demonstration—and installs it for the current user so its files remain separate from RPM-managed Python locations.

commands.explanation: Uses Python 3.12's pip to install pipx under the current user's home directory instead of the system Python package directories.
Invokes pipx through Python directly to confirm the installation before relying on the standalone command's PATH entry.

steps.expected: pip installs pipx and its dependencies under the current user's home directory, and `python3.12 -m pipx` reports its version.
steps.troubleshooting: Use the failing command to distinguish package-index access during installation from failure to import or start the installed pipx application.

recovery.symptom: pip cannot reach or trust the package index
recovery.detail: Correct DNS, HTTPS proxy, trusted-certificate, or system-time configuration and retry this user-scoped installation. Do not add --break-system-packages.

recovery.symptom: Python cannot start the installed pipx module
recovery.detail: Inspect pipx through the same Python 3.12 interpreter used for installation, then repeat the module-based version check.
recovery.command:
python3.12 -m pip show pipx
python3.12 -m pipx --version

steps.label: Configure PATH
steps.title: Add user-installed commands to PATH
steps.alt: Terminal adding the user application directory to PATH and locating pipx
steps.explanation: User-scoped Python applications place their launchers in the user's local bin directory. Add that directory to Bash startup configuration so pipx and the commands it exposes remain available in later shells.

commands.explanation: Appends the user application directory to Bash's PATH configuration. The single quotes preserve the variables for expansion when the file is sourced.
Reloads the updated Bash configuration in the current shell without requiring a logout.
Shows the exact pipx launcher selected from PATH; it should resolve under ~/.local/bin.
Confirms that the standalone command starts successfully after the PATH change.

steps.expected: pipx resolves to ~/.local/bin/pipx and reports its installed version.
steps.note: Run the echo command once. Repeating it adds duplicate PATH lines to .bashrc, although the resulting PATH still works.
steps.troubleshooting: Use the shell startup file and command path to distinguish a missing PATH entry from a duplicate entry added by repeating this step.

recovery.symptom: pipx is still not available on PATH
recovery.detail: Inspect the saved PATH line, reload the Bash configuration, and confirm which pipx launcher the shell selects.
recovery.command:
tail -n 5 ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
command -v pipx
pipx --version

recovery.symptom: The PATH line appears more than once
recovery.detail: Use the line-numbered output to identify duplicate entries. Keep one correct export line and edit the shell startup file carefully before sourcing it again.
recovery.command: grep -nF 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' ~/.bashrc

steps.label: Install ansible-core
steps.title: Install upstream ansible-core with pipx
steps.alt: Terminal showing pipx installing ansible-core 2.21 with Python 3.12
steps.explanation: pipx creates and manages an application-specific virtual environment, installs the requested upstream distribution into it, and exposes its command-line entry points through the user's local bin directory.

commands.explanation: Creates a pipx-managed environment with Python 3.12 and installs the newest available maintenance release in the ansible-core 2.21 feature line from PyPI.

steps.expected: pipx installs ansible-core 2.21.x with Python 3.12 and lists the Ansible commands made available on the user's PATH.
steps.note: The feature-line constraint lets this demonstration select the newest available 2.21 maintenance release. For a repeatable environment, replace it with the exact release accepted during testing and record the resolved dependencies. A warning that setuptools is absent from pipx's shared libraries does not indicate an ansible-core installation failure.
steps.troubleshooting: Use pipx's result to distinguish an unavailable ansible-core release from a successfully created environment whose command launchers are not reachable through PATH.

recovery.symptom: No matching ansible-core release is found
recovery.detail: Confirm the Python and pipx versions, then review the releases visible through the configured package index before changing the requested feature line.
recovery.command:
python3.12 --version
pipx --version
python3.12 -m pip index versions ansible-core

recovery.symptom: pipx installs the environment but Ansible commands are unavailable
recovery.detail: Confirm that pipx lists the environment and that the user application directory is still present in PATH.
recovery.command:
pipx list
command -v ansible
printf '%s\n' "$PATH"

steps.label: Verify Isolation
steps.title: Verify pipx isolation and package provenance
steps.alt: Terminal proving that ansible-core is isolated by pipx and not installed as an RPM
steps.explanation: A version number alone does not prove how software was installed. Check pipx's managed environments, the RPM database, executable location, Python metadata, dependency health, and Ansible runtime together.

commands.explanation: Lists pipx-managed environments, their Python versions, and the command-line applications exposed on PATH.
Confirms that the RHEL ansible-core RPM remains absent after the upstream installation.
Shows that the active Ansible launcher comes from the user's local bin directory.
Runs pip inside the pipx-managed ansible-core environment and displays the package version, dependencies, and installation location.
Checks that the isolated environment has no missing or incompatible Python package requirements.
Reports the active ansible-core release, executable path, Python runtime, and content search paths.

steps.expected: pipx reports ansible-core 2.21.x under ~/.local/share/pipx, RPM reports no ansible-core package, dependencies are healthy, and ansible runs through Python 3.12.
steps.troubleshooting: Check each result independently: pipx ownership, RPM absence, launcher resolution, package metadata, dependency health, and the active ansible-core runtime.

recovery.symptom: Ansible resolves to the wrong launcher
recovery.detail: List every matching command and the pipx environment before changing PATH or any installation.
recovery.command:
type -a ansible
command -v ansible
pipx list

recovery.symptom: An ansible-core RPM is unexpectedly installed
recovery.detail: Do not remove it automatically. Record both installations and decide which package owner should provide the active command.
recovery.command:
rpm -q ansible-core
type -a ansible

recovery.symptom: pipx does not list the ansible-core environment
recovery.detail: Confirm pipx's configured locations and inventory before deciding whether this installation step must be repeated.
recovery.command:
pipx environment
pipx list

recovery.symptom: pipx reports broken Python requirements
recovery.detail: Save the conflict and inspect packages inside this application environment before repairing or recreating only the pipx-managed environment.
recovery.command:
pipx runpip ansible-core check
pipx runpip ansible-core list

steps.label: Record Baseline
steps.title: Record and pin the pipx application baseline
steps.alt: Terminal recording the pipx-managed ansible-core environment, its resolved Python packages, and successful pin status
steps.explanation: A pipx environment is isolated, but isolation alone does not make its contents repeatable. Record the pipx version, application, interpreter, exposed commands, and resolved Python packages, then pin the accepted application so routine pipx upgrade and reinstall operations do not change it unintentionally.

commands.explanation: Records the pipx version that owns the application environment and starts a fresh baseline file while keeping the version visible in the terminal.
Appends the pipx-managed application, Python interpreter, environment location, exposed commands, and any injected packages while keeping the same inventory visible in the terminal.
Runs pip inside the ansible-core application environment and saves every resolved Python package and exact version as an installable requirements baseline.
Pins the accepted ansible-core application against pipx upgrade and reinstall operations and appends machine-readable confirmation to the baseline file.

steps.expected: The terminal and ~/ansible-core-pipx-baseline.txt identify the pipx version, managed application, interpreter, exposed commands, and successful pin; ~/ansible-core-pipx-requirements.txt records the exact Python package set.
steps.note: A pipx pin controls pipx upgrade and reinstall operations; it is not a portable lock file and does not freeze collections, configuration, inventory, credentials, Python wheels, or operating-system libraries. Review and unpin the application deliberately when approving an update.
steps.troubleshooting: Treat pipx version capture, application inventory, dependency capture, and pinning as separate checks. The pipx command and managed environment must remain healthy before the baseline can be accepted.

recovery.symptom: pipx cannot report its version or find the ansible-core environment
recovery.detail: Confirm the pipx launcher and version, then inspect its configured paths and application inventory before repeating this baseline step.
recovery.command:
command -v pipx
pipx --version
pipx environment
pipx list --include-injected

recovery.symptom: The dependency capture fails
recovery.detail: Check the application environment's Python requirements and package inventory before accepting or recreating its baseline.
recovery.command:
pipx runpip ansible-core check
pipx runpip ansible-core list

recovery.symptom: The pin result is not successful
recovery.detail: Confirm the pipx application name, then repeat the pin command and require a successful result before treating the application as held.
recovery.command:
pipx list
pipx pin ansible-core --output json

steps.label: Reproduce Baseline
steps.title: Recreate the recorded pipx application baseline
steps.alt: Terminal recreating the pipx-managed ansible-core application from its exact recorded Python package baseline and restoring its pin
steps.explanation: Use the recorded application specification and exact Python package baseline to recreate the pipx environment through the same package owner. Verify the rebuilt inventory before restoring the application pin and accepting the runtime.

commands.explanation: Stores the portable path to the exact pipx requirements baseline in a short shell variable used throughout the rebuild.
Stores a separate portable path for the recreated environment's package inventory.
Reads the exact ansible-core package specification from the saved requirements baseline into a shell variable.
Removes the pipx hold deliberately so the accepted application environment can be replaced during this controlled rebuild.
Removes only the pipx-managed ansible-core application environment and its exposed launchers; the recorded baseline files remain available.
Recreates the application with Python 3.12, the exact ansible-core release, and the full recorded dependency set.
Captures the complete package inventory from the recreated pipx environment in a separate comparison file.
Compares the rebuilt package inventory with the accepted baseline byte for byte and prints confirmation only when they match.
Restores the pipx pin and returns machine-readable confirmation that the rebuilt application is held against routine upgrade or reinstall operations.
Confirms that the recreated application exposes a working ansible-core command through the expected pipx launcher and Python runtime.

steps.expected: pipx recreates ansible-core with Python 3.12, the comparison prints Verified, the pin result reports success, and ansible --version resolves through the pipx-managed environment.
steps.note: The rebuild depends on the exact releases remaining available from the configured package index. It does not preserve wheel artifacts, pipx itself, Python, system libraries, collections, configuration, inventory, credentials, or managed-host dependencies. Retain approved artifacts when later recovery must not depend on a live index.
steps.troubleshooting: Treat the saved specification, unpin and uninstall operations, package availability, exact comparison, restored pin, and executable path as separate checks. Do not loosen recorded versions merely to make the rebuild succeed.

recovery.symptom: The exact ansible-core specification is empty
recovery.detail: Confirm that the requirements baseline exists and contains one ansible-core entry before uninstalling the accepted application.
recovery.command: grep '^ansible-core==' "$HOME/ansible-core-pipx-requirements.txt"

recovery.symptom: An exact package version is unavailable
recovery.detail: Keep the baseline unchanged and confirm package-index access. A controlled mirror or retained wheel set may be required to reproduce this application later.
recovery.command:
python3.12 -m pip config list
python3.12 -m pip index versions ansible-core

recovery.symptom: The package comparison does not print Verified
recovery.detail: Capture the rebuilt inventory and compare it with the accepted baseline before restoring the pin or using the application.
recovery.command:
pipx runpip ansible-core freeze --all > "$HOME/ansible-core-pipx-rebuild.txt"
diff -u "$HOME/ansible-core-pipx-requirements.txt" "$HOME/ansible-core-pipx-rebuild.txt"

recovery.symptom: The pin or runtime verification fails
recovery.detail: Inspect the recreated pipx environment, its dependency health, and the exposed executable before deciding whether to repeat the rebuild.
recovery.command:
pipx list --include-injected
pipx runpip ansible-core check
command -v ansible

steps.label: Inspect Content
steps.title: Inspect the upstream content boundary
steps.alt: Terminal showing no separately installed collections and the embedded ansible.builtin namespace
steps.explanation: Prepare the standard user collection path, then compare separately installed collection artifacts with the module documentation embedded in ansible-core. This exposes the ansible.builtin content boundary without triggering an empty-path warning.

commands.explanation: Creates the standard user collection directory so a clean installation can be inspected without a missing-path warning.
Lists collection artifacts discovered in configured collection paths. A clean environment may have no separately installed collections.
Prints the available module documentation while omitting a known internal collection-discovery warning from this focused display.
Counts the displayed module documentation entries. The number can change between ansible-core releases.
Prints the concise argument summary for the ansible.builtin.ping module without opening an interactive pager.

steps.expected: The collection path is prepared, no separately installed collection is required, and ansible-doc lists the available modules and displays help for ansible.builtin.ping.
steps.note: The stderr redirection keeps a known ansible._protomatter collection-discovery warning out of this focused display; it does not change the module list or count. The ansible.builtin namespace is embedded in ansible-core and is not listed as a separately installed collection.
steps.troubleshooting: Separate collection-directory permissions, unexpected collection namespaces, and failure to load the embedded ansible.builtin.ping documentation.

recovery.symptom: The collection directory cannot be created
recovery.detail: Inspect ownership and permissions under the current user's .ansible directory before repeating the mkdir command.
recovery.command:
ls -ld ~/.ansible ~/.ansible/collections 2>/dev/null
mkdir -p ~/.ansible/collections/ansible_collections

recovery.symptom: Additional collection namespaces appear
recovery.detail: Use the active collection paths and collection inventory to decide whether the additional content is intentional; do not delete shared content merely to match the demo.
recovery.command:
ansible --version
ansible-galaxy collection list

recovery.symptom: ansible.builtin.ping documentation cannot be loaded
recovery.detail: Confirm the active ansible-doc executable belongs to this installation, then repeat the FQCN documentation lookup.
recovery.command:
command -v ansible-doc
PAGER=cat ansible-doc -s ansible.builtin.ping

steps.label: Test Ansible
steps.title: Run a functional localhost smoke test
steps.alt: Terminal showing the pipx-managed Ansible runtime returning pong from localhost
steps.explanation: Finish with an end-to-end execution check. The ansible command runs in pipx's Python 3.12 environment, while ansible.builtin.ping executes locally with RHEL's system Python to avoid an interpreter-discovery warning.

commands.explanation: Runs the ansible.builtin.ping module against an inline localhost inventory through the local connection and explicitly selects the managed-host Python interpreter. This tests Python module execution rather than network ICMP.

steps.expected: localhost returns SUCCESS with changed: false and ping: pong, without an interpreter-discovery warning.
steps.note: You now have a working local ansible-core runtime. Remote managed-host readiness has not yet been tested.
steps.troubleshooting: This step depends only on the pipx-managed Ansible command, the explicitly selected managed-host Python, and local execution of ansible.builtin.ping.

recovery.symptom: The selected managed-host Python does not exist
recovery.detail: Confirm the path used by this command. Do not substitute a different interpreter until its compatibility with the managed host has been established.
recovery.command:
ls -l /usr/bin/python3
/usr/bin/python3 --version

recovery.symptom: Ansible resolves outside the pipx installation
recovery.detail: Confirm the selected launcher and pipx environment before repeating the smoke test.
recovery.command:
type -a ansible
command -v ansible
pipx list

recovery.symptom: pipx reports an unhealthy environment
recovery.detail: Inspect this environment's dependency report and package list before repairing or recreating it.
recovery.command:
pipx runpip ansible-core check
pipx runpip ansible-core list

recovery.symptom: localhost does not return pong
recovery.detail: Repeat only this step's command after the interpreter and launcher checks pass. Continue when localhost reports SUCCESS and pong.
recovery.command: ansible localhost -i localhost, -m ansible.builtin.ping -c local -e ansible_python_interpreter=/usr/bin/python3

verification: rhc status reports active Subscription Management and Red Hat Lightspeed connections
BaseOS and AppStream are enabled for the system architecture
Python 3.12 and pip were installed from subscribed RHEL AppStream repositories
pipx is installed for the current user and available through ~/.local/bin
rpm reports that the RHEL ansible-core package is not installed
The saved pipx inventory and requirements baselines record the pipx version, application, interpreter, exposed commands, exact Python packages, and successful pin status
The pipx application is recreated through pipx, its exact package comparison passes, and the pin is restored
The embedded ansible.builtin module documentation is available without separately installed collections
The localhost ansible.builtin.ping test returns SUCCESS and ping: pong

completionRecord.maintenancePath: Use pipx to inspect, upgrade, pin, or remove the isolated application environment. Do not modify it with the system Python, DNF, or an unrelated pip command.

items.label: ansible-core version
items.value: [paste the version reported by pipx list]

items.label: pipx baseline reproduction
items.value: Application recreated through pipx · exact package comparison passed · pin restored

cleanup.explanation: This removes the pipx-managed ansible-core application but intentionally retains ~/ansible-core-pipx-baseline.txt and ~/ansible-core-pipx-requirements.txt as evidence. It also leaves pipx, Python 3.12, the ~/.local/bin PATH entry in ~/.bashrc, and the user collection directory available for other tools. Remove those shared prerequisites or settings only after checking their other users and local policy. Disconnect RHEL only when this disposable VM will not be used for later labs. For an organization-managed system, complete the applicable inventory, subscription, security, and asset-retirement process as well.
cleanup.command:
pipx uninstall ansible-core
# Optional: disconnect this disposable lab VM
sudo rhc disconnect
